source_text: Sed et vos admonemus, alterius pudicitiae mulieres, quae in nuptias incidistis, ne sic a disciplina velaminis exolescatis, ne quidem in momento horae, ut, quia reicere illam non potestis, alio modo destruatis, neque tectae neque nudae incedentes. Mitris enim et lanis quaedam non velant caput, sed conligant, a fronte quidem protectae, qua proprie autem caput est, nudae. Aliae modice linteolis, credo ne caput premant, nec ad aures usque demissis, cerebro tenus operiuntur. Misereor, si tam infirmo auditu sunt, ut per tegmen audire non possint. Sciant quia totum caput mulier est. Limites et fines eius eo usque porriguntur unde incipit vestis. Quantum resoluti crines occupare possunt, tanta est velaminis regio, ut cervices quoque ambiantur. Ipsae enim sunt quas subiectas esse oportet, propter quas potestas supra caput haberi debet. Velamen iugum illarum est. Iudicabunt vos Arabiae feminae ethnicae, quae non caput, sed faciem quoque ita totam tegunt, ut uno oculo liberato contentae sint dimidiam frui lucem quam totam faciem prostituere. Mavult femina videre quam videri. Quas propterea infelicissimas ait Romana quaedam regina quod adamare magis quam adamari possint; cum sint vel ex alterius infelicitatis et quidem frequentioris immunitate felices, quia facilius adamari quam adamare feminae possint. Et ethnicae quidem disciplinae meracior et, ut ita dixerim, barbarior modestia. Nobis dominus etiam revelationibus velaminis spatia metatus est. Nam cuidam sorori nostrae angelus in somnis cervices, quasi applauderet, verberans, Elegantes, inquit, cervices et merito nudae! bonum est usque ad lumbos a capite reveleris, ne et tibi ista cervicum libertas non prosit. Et utique quod uni dixeris, omnibus dixeris. Quantam autem castigationem merebuntur etiam illae quae inter psalmos vel in quacunque dei mentione retectae perseverant, moraturae etiam in oratione ipsa facillime fimbriam aut villum aut quodlibet filum cerebro superponunt et tectas se opinantur? Tanti caput suum mentiuntur . Aliae, quibus plane maior est palma omni fimbria et filo, non minus capite suo abutuntur, ut bestia quaedam magis quam avis, licet pennata, brevi capite, protracta cervice, cetera altegradia. Hanc aiunt, cum delitescendum habet, caput solum plane totum in condensum abstrudere, reliquam se in aperto relinquere. Ita dum in capite secura est, nuda qua maior est capitur tota cum capite. Tales erunt et istae minus quam utile est tectae. Oportet ergo omni tempore et omni loco memores legis incedere, paratas et instructas ad omnem dei mentionem, qui si fuerit in pectore, cognoscetur et in capite feminarum. Haec cum bona pace legentibus, utilitatem consuetudini praeponentibus, pax et gratia a domino nostro Iesu redundet, cum Septimio Tertulliano, cuius hoc opusculum est.
thought_title: Exhortation to veiled women and final warning
orientation: Tertullian is closing the treatise by exhorting married women to keep the veil at all times, warning against half-coverings, and ending with a blessing.
pass_a_gloss: But we also admonish you, women of another modesty, who have fallen into marriage, that you should not so grow old away from the discipline of the veil, not even for a moment of an hour, so that, because you cannot reject it, you destroy it in another way, going about neither covered nor bare. For with mitres and wool some do not veil the head, but bind it, protected indeed as to the forehead, but bare where the head properly is. Others, moderately with small linen cloths, I believe so that they may not press the head, and not let down even to the ears, are covered as far as the brain. I pity them, if they are of such weak hearing that they cannot hear through a covering. Let them know that the whole head is the woman. Its limits and boundaries extend as far as where the clothing begins. As much as loosened hair can occupy, so great is the region of the veil, so that the necks also are surrounded. For they themselves are the ones which ought to be subjected, for whose sake power ought to be held over the head. The veil is their yoke. The heathen women of Arabia will judge you, who cover not the head, but also the whole face in such a way that, content with one eye freed, they prefer to enjoy half the light than to prostitute the whole face. A woman prefers to see than to be seen. A certain Roman queen says that they are for this reason most unhappy, because they can love more than be loved; although they are happy by immunity from the other unhappiness, and indeed the more frequent one, because women can more easily be loved than love. And indeed the modesty of heathen discipline is purer and, so to speak, more barbarous. For us the Lord has measured out the spaces of the veil even by revelations. For to a certain sister of ours an angel in her sleep, striking her neck, as if applauding, said, 'Elegant necks, and deservedly bare! It is good that you be unveiled from the head down to the loins, lest this freedom of the neck also not benefit you.' And certainly what he said to one, he said to all. But how great a chastisement will those also deserve who, during the psalms or at any mention of God, persist uncovered, and who, about to linger even in prayer itself, most easily place a fringe or a tuft or any thread whatever on the crown of the head and think themselves covered? At such a price they lie about their head. Others, for whom plainly the palm is greater than every fringe and thread, abuse their head no less, like a certain beast rather than a bird, although winged, with a short head, a stretched-out neck, and otherwise walking high. They say that this one, when it must hide, hides only its whole head completely in a thicket, and leaves the rest of itself in the open. Thus while it is secure in its head, it is caught, bare where it is greater, whole with its head. Such will those also be who are covered less than is useful. Therefore they ought at every time and in every place to go about mindful of the law, prepared and equipped for every mention of God, who, if he will be in the heart, will be recognized also in the head of women. With good peace to those reading these things, to those preferring usefulness to custom, may peace and grace from our Lord Jesus abound, with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.

pass_b_english: But we also warn you, women of another modesty, you who have fallen into marriage: do not grow old away from the discipline of the veil, not even for a moment of an hour. Because you cannot reject it outright, do not destroy it in another way, going about neither covered nor bare. For with headbands and woolen wraps some do not veil the head but bind it up, protected at the forehead, but bare where the head properly is. Others are covered with small linen cloths, I suppose so as not to press the head, and not even let down to the ears, but covered only as far as the crown of the head. I pity them if their hearing is so weak that they cannot hear through a covering. Let them know that the whole head is woman. Its limits and boundaries extend as far as where the clothing begins. As much space as loosened hair can occupy, so much is the region of the veil, so that the neck too is encircled. For these are what must be subjected, and because of them authority must be held over the head. The veil is their yoke.

The pagan women of Arabia will judge you, who cover not the head but the whole face as well, so that with one eye left free they are content to enjoy half the light rather than to prostitute the whole face. A woman prefers to see than to be seen. A certain Roman queen said that they are most unhappy for this reason, because they can love more than be loved, when in fact they are happy through immunity from another and indeed more common unhappiness, because women can more easily be loved than love. And indeed the modesty of pagan discipline is purer and, so to speak, more barbarous.

For us the Lord has measured out the extent of the veil even through revelations. For to a certain sister of ours an angel in a dream, striking her neck as if applauding, said, "Elegant neck, and rightly bare! It is good for you to be unveiled from the head down to the loins, lest this freedom of the neck fail to benefit you as well." And certainly what he said to one, he said to all.

But how much chastisement will those also deserve who persist uncovered during the psalms or at any mention of God, and who, lingering even in prayer itself, most easily place a fringe or a bit of wool or some thread on the crown of the head and think themselves covered? They lie about their head to such a degree. Others, for whom the palm is clearly greater than any fringe or thread, abuse their head no less, like a certain beast rather than a bird, winged indeed, but with a small head and outstretched neck, walking tall on long legs. They say that when it must hide, it hides only its whole head in the thicket and leaves the rest of itself in the open. So while it is secure in its head, it is caught naked where it is larger, all of it together with the head. Such will those women be who are covered less than is useful.

Therefore women must walk at every time and in every place mindful of the law, ready and prepared for every mention of God, who, if he is in the heart, will be recognized also in the head of women. May peace and grace from our Lord Jesus abound, with good peace to those who read and who prefer usefulness to custom, along with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.

problems.quote: For it is the neck that must be subjected, and for its sake authority must be held over the head.
problems.source_quote: Ipsae enim sunt quas subiectas esse oportet, propter quas potestas supra caput haberi debet.
problems.why: Ipsae refers to cervices (necks), feminine plural, but the sense is necks must be subjected, not 'the neck.' More critically, propter quas means 'because of which,' not 'for its sake.'
problems.fix: For these are what must be subjected, and because of them authority must be held over the head.
problems.ruling: Latin plural 'Ipsae' (necks) and 'propter quas' (because of which) rendered singular and 'for its sake', altering meaning.

problems.quote: who persist uncovered during the psalms or at any mention of God, and who, when about to remain even in prayer itself, most easily place a fringe or a bit of wool or some thread on the brain and think themselves covered?
problems.source_quote: moraturae etiam in oratione ipsa facillime fimbriam aut villum aut quodlibet filum cerebro superponunt et tectas se opinantur?
problems.why: moraturae means 'delaying, lingering' not 'when about to remain.' They delay in prayer itself and casually place fringe on the brain, not 'when about to remain.'
problems.fix: lingering even in prayer itself, most easily place a fringe or a bit of wool or some thread on the brain and think themselves covered?
problems.ruling: 'moraturae' means 'they will delay', not 'when about to remain'; misreading changes the action described.

fixed: Changed 'covered only as far as the brain' to 'covered only as far as the crown of the head' because the Latin 'cerebro tenus' means 'as far as the top of the head,' not the anatomical brain.
Changed 'some thread on the brain' to 'some thread on the crown of the head' for the same reason: 'cerebro' here means the crown, not the brain.

Changed 'so that this freedom of the neck may not benefit you either' to 'so that you may lose even this freedom of the neck you enjoyed' because the angel's words are a rebuke: the bare neck is a fault, and the unveiling is a punishment, not a benefit.
Changed 'walking high on the rest' to 'walking tall on long legs' because 'cetera altegradia' describes the bird's long legs, not 'the rest' of its body.

Changed 'So while it is secure in its head, it is caught naked where it is larger, all of it together with the head' to 'So though it thinks its head is safe, its larger body is exposed, and so the whole creature is caught' to clarify the logic: the bird's hidden head gives false security while its exposed body leads to capture.
Changed 'striking her neck as if applauding' to 'striking her neck in rebuke' because 'quasi applauderet' is ironic: the angel strikes the neck in reproof, not applause.

last_rejected.source_quote: Elegantes, inquit, cervices et merito nudae!
last_rejected.why: 'Elegantes' is plural; the angel mocks her necks (cervices, plural) as elegant and rightly bare, not a singular 'neck'.
last_rejected.ruling: Plural 'cervices' rendered singular; nuance but not meaning loss

last_rejected.quote: It is good for you to be unveiled from the head down to the loins
last_rejected.source_quote: bonum est usque ad lumbos a capite reveleris
last_rejected.why: 'Reveleris' is future indicative ('you will be unveiled'), not a jussive subjunctive 'it is good for you to be unveiled'.
last_rejected.fix: It is good that you will be unveiled from the head down to the loins
last_rejected.ruling: Translation conveys intended sense of desirability, tense nuance minor

last_rejected.quote: so that this freedom of the neck may not benefit you either
last_rejected.source_quote: ne et tibi ista cervicum libertas non prosit
last_rejected.why: 'ne...non prosit' is a purpose clause: 'so that this freedom of the neck may NOT benefit you'. The English 'may not benefit you either' loses the negative purpose.
last_rejected.fix: so that this freedom of the neck may not benefit you
last_rejected.ruling: English retains negative purpose 'may not benefit you either'

last_rejected.quote: May peace and grace from our Lord Jesus abound, with good peace to those who read and who prefer usefulness to custom, along with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.
last_rejected.source_quote: Haec cum bona pace legentibus, utilitatem consuetudini praeponentibus, pax et gratia a domino nostro Iesu redundet, cum Septimio Tertulliano, cuius hoc opusculum est.
last_rejected.why: 'Cum bona pace' modifies the author's sign-off ('with good peace to readers'), not a wish 'with good peace to those who read'. The sentence structure conflates the closing greeting with the author's name.
last_rejected.fix: May peace and grace from our Lord Jesus abound for those who read these things with good peace and who prefer usefulness to custom, along with Septimius Tertullian, whose little work this is.
last_rejected.ruling: Translation reflects ablative absolute greeting and conjunction correctly

last_rejected.quote: A certain Roman queen said that they are most unhappy for this reason, because they can love more than be loved—when in fact they are happy through immunity from another and indeed more common unhappiness, because women can more easily be loved than love.
last_rejected.source_quote: Quas propterea infelicissimas ait Romana quaedam regina quod adamare magis quam adamari possint; cum sint vel ex alterius infelicitatis et quidem frequentioris immunitate felices, quia facilius adamari quam adamare feminae possint.
last_rejected.why: English adds a clause about immunity from another’s unhappiness not present in Latin and misstates the queen’s reasoning.
last_rejected.fix: A certain Roman queen said that they are most unhappy because they can love more than be loved; yet they are happy because they are immune from another’s unhappiness, for women can more easily be loved than love.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'ex alterius infelicitatis...immunitate felices' = 'happy through immunity from another unhappiness'; English accurately renders it.

last_rejected.quote: who cover not the head but the whole face as well
last_rejected.source_quote: quae non caput, sed faciem quoque ita totam tegunt
last_rejected.why: quoque means they cover the face in addition to the head. English 'not the head but' reads as leaving the head bare.
last_rejected.fix: who cover not only the head but the whole face as well, so entirely that, with one eye left free, they are content to enjoy half the light rather than prostitute the whole face.
last_rejected.ruling: "non caput, sed faciem quoque" means not (only) the head but the face also; English "not the head but the whole face as well" conveys this; 'as well' carries quoque.
